description: We are Redalaxy, a team of young innovators dedicated to developing creative solutions. Our space mission is to share the stories of forgotten objects in space, helping people discover their original purpose, their history, and the benefits they brought to humanity.
summary: Metallic Space is a webpage that displays technical and scientific information to a non-specialist audience, making astronomical facts accessible to the general public. Our solution directly addresses the given challenge since the objects displayed are artifacts abandoned in Earth's orbit, devices that have already completed their purposes or ended up broken. This gives those objects a second purpose: to tell their stories and provide insight into what humanity has done. The relevance of the project lies in how people currently engage with scientific information considering that finding the information we display normally requires significant hours of research and a deep understanding of technical terms. Hence, we offer a straightforward solution to bring these forgotten space artifacts back into the public eye, transforming raw orbital data into an interactive experience anyone can explore and understand.
details:
Metallic Earth

What does it do or how does it work?

Metallic Space is an interactive 3D web application that shows Earth surrounded by real human-made objects that are still orbiting our planet. The system gathers information on ten real space artifacts from NASA’s NSSDCA and CelesTrak, organizes it into verified records, and presents each one as a clear information card with its catalog ID, owner, launch year, mission, current status, and importance, written for people with no astronomy background. Users can rotate the Earth, zoom in, select an object, and read its card. Objects are placed around the Earth for illustration only, so their positions do not reflect their real orbits. Our metaphor is artistic: space debris as the stars and particles of an artificial galaxy created by humanity, while the data behind it stays scientific and verifiable.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefits are accessibility and reliability. Existing catalogs are accurate but hard to read for non-specialists, so Metallic Space turns them into something people can explore: instead of reading a table, users rotate the Earth, pick an object, and read about it, which makes the topic easier to remember. It focuses on satellites that are still in orbit, so users learn about real objects that are up there right now, not just historical cases. Every fact on a card comes from public, open data with its source cited, so users can check it themselves. It runs in a browser on a computer with nothing to install, and it is scalable: adding a new object only means adding a data record and a card.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is for people to see space debris as something real and close, not an abstract problem. By turning technical catalog data into a visual, explorable experience, we hope to raise awareness about orbital safety and the long-term sustainability of space activity, and to encourage curiosity about the science behind it. Metallic Space can serve as an educational tool in classrooms, museums, or outreach projects, and can later grow with more objects and more features.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We built the interface and information cards with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. For the 3D Earth we used Model Viewer, an open-source web component created by Google for displaying 3D models directly on web pages. We researched each object in NASA’s NSSDCA (NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive) and CelesTrak. The project runs on standard laptops.

How is your project creative?

Most debris tools look like technical dashboards. We took a different approach: treating human-made objects as the stars of a “metallic galaxy” around the Earth. This changes how people see the problem, because debris becomes something to explore instead of a list of numbers. The creative layer never replaces the science. Every object is backed by real catalog data and sources, so the artistic concept makes the information more memorable without making it less accurate.

What factors did your team consider?

We put scientific rigor first and usability second. We did not invent dimensions, masses, or operating conditions, and every data point needs a source. We checked which objects are still in orbit, which were destroyed, and which re-entered, and for fragmented satellites we used a cataloged fragment with available data. To keep the visuals honest, we used images from official NASA sources to show what each satellite looks like, and we state that object placement is illustrative. We also designed for accessibility, with clear labels and easy navigation. The work was split across research and programming.
